title: Rose and the Stolen Supper Spell
paragraphs: "Daddy, the pasta pesto is GONE," said Rose.
Not just gone from the bowl — gone from the whole city of Amsterdam.
Every pot, every pan, every single noodle.
Rose pressed her nose to the kitchen window and saw the canal boats sitting very still, and all the people looking very confused.
Daddy ran in from the hallway, his curly brown hair sticking up on one side.
"Gone?" he said.
"But I made it fresh this morning."
Then they both saw it: a trail of green pesto footprints leading out the front door, down the steps, and all the way to the edge of the Enchanted Forest at the end of the street.
Rose grabbed Daddy's hand.
"We're going in."
Daddy smoothed his short beard the way he always did when he was thinking hard.
"Right," he said.
"Together, then."
The Enchanted Forest smelled like pine needles and something faintly cheesy.
The trees had silver bark and the mushrooms glowed a soft orange.
Rose kept her eyes on the pesto footprints.
They went left past a sleeping fox, right past a badger with muddy knees, and straight toward a crooked little cottage with smoke coming out of the chimney.
Through the window, Rose could see him.
Bad Man Matt.
He was wearing his white doctor's coat, which was already covered in green smears.
His white hair was wild.
His face looked like a man who had not slept well in about fifteen years.
He was stirring an enormous pot and cackling to himself in a very tired sort of way.
"All the pasta pesto in Amsterdam," he muttered, "and I shall eat it for DESSERT."
"That's not even a dessert," Daddy whispered.
"Shh," said Rose.
She had a plan.
She knocked on the door — three sharp knocks.
Bad Man Matt opened it.
He blinked at Rose.
He blinked at Daddy.
He looked back at his pot.
"I am a doctor," he said, as if that explained everything.
"I know," said Rose.
"And doctors have to wash their hands before eating.
Those are the rules."
Bad Man Matt looked at his hands.
They were extremely green.
"I suppose," he said slowly, "that is true."
He shuffled off to find the sink, which was around the back of the cottage and apparently very far away, because they could hear him muttering about it for quite some time.
Rose and Daddy stepped inside.
The pot was enormous — far too big to carry.
Rose looked at Daddy.
Daddy looked at Rose.
"The recipe," Rose said.
"If we have the recipe, we can make more."
Daddy spotted a crumpled piece of paper pinned to the wall.
He reached up and unpinned it.
It was written in loopy old handwriting: THE SPELL FOR PASTA PESTO THAT STAYS WARM FOREVER.
That was when Bad Man Matt came back.
"HEY," he said.
He lunged for the recipe.
Daddy stepped sideways.
Bad Man Matt tripped on his own doctor's coat and sat down very hard in a basket of pine cones.
"Ow," he said.
Rose and Daddy ran.
They ran through the silver trees, past the glowing mushrooms, past the badger with muddy knees who watched them go with great interest.
They ran all the way back to the canal, back up the steps, back into the kitchen.
Daddy cooked.
Rose stood on her stool and stirred.
The whole apartment filled with the smell of basil and garlic and something warm and good.
When the bowls were on the table and the pasta was perfectly twisted around the fork, Rose took one bite.
It was exactly right.
Daddy sat across from her, a little pesto on his beard, smiling in the quiet way he did when everything was fine.
Outside, the canal boats began to move again.
And somewhere in the Enchanted Forest, Bad Man Matt was still sitting in the pine cones, thinking about dessert.

title: The Tiger in the Racing Seat
paragraphs: Santosh's racing car had two seats, four shiny wheels, and one very serious problem.
His co-driver kept falling over.
"Tiger," Santosh said, "you have to watch the road."
His cuddly orange tiger leaned against the door.
One soft paw rested on the window.
He looked extremely comfortable.
Santosh fastened the little seat belt across Tiger's tummy.
Now the toy sat straight, with his black stripes showing and his stitched smile facing the track.
"Much better."
Dad checked Santosh's helmet and tightened his own glove around the little car's safety strap.
"Three laps," he said.
"Stay on the track, and stop if you need help."
Santosh nodded.
Beyond the starting line, the racecourse curled around the park.
There was a wooden bridge, a bend beside the flower beds, and a finish line hung with colorful flags.
A girl in a green car pulled up beside him.
"I'm Maya," she said.
"Who's that?"
"Tiger.
He's my co-driver."
Maya considered Tiger's steady smile.
"He looks fast."
The starter raised a flag.
Three.
Two.
One.
Go!
Santosh pressed the pedal.
The car rolled forward, then faster.
Wind slipped around his helmet.
Tiger's ears fluttered.
Over the wooden bridge they went.
Rumble, rumble, rumble.
Around the flower beds they swept.
The flags flashed red and yellow ahead.
Maya's green car was just in front.
"We can catch her," Santosh told Tiger.
They passed the starting line.
Two laps to go.
On the bridge, something bounced against Santosh's elbow.
Tiger's striped tail.
Santosh glanced at it.
The car drifted toward the edge of the track.
He looked up quickly and straightened the wheel.
"Road first," he whispered.
At the flower-bed bend, a yellow cone lay across the narrowest part of the track.
Maya braked.
Santosh pressed his brake too.
Their cars stopped with a small space between them.
"We could drive on the grass," Maya said.
Santosh looked at the soft ground.
Yesterday's rain had left a dark muddy patch beside the bend.
"We'd get stuck."
He raised his hand.
At the edge of the course, Dad spotted him and waved to the race helper.
The helper lifted the fallen cone and set it upright.
"Good stopping," she said.
"Ready?"
Maya nodded.
Santosh checked Tiger's seat belt.
Off they went again.
This time Santosh watched the bend all the way through.
He turned smoothly, keeping his hands steady.
Maya was still ahead, but not by much.
One lap to go.
The bridge rumbled beneath them.
Santosh felt every bump through his seat.
Tiger bounced once, safely strapped in, and settled against the cushion.
At the final bend, Santosh started turning a little earlier.
The car followed the curve without wobbling.
He came out beside Maya.
The finish flags fluttered closer.
Dad was cheering.
Someone rang a bell.
Santosh pressed the pedal and kept his eyes straight ahead.
Maya crossed the line first.
Santosh crossed one heartbeat later.
He let the car slow to a stop.
For a moment he stared at the flags.
Then Maya turned around.
"Your tiger didn't even blink!"
Santosh looked at his co-driver.
Tiger was still smiling his stitched smile, with both paws pointed forward.
"He's been practicing," Santosh said.
Dad came over and lifted Santosh's helmet.
His hair sprang up underneath.
"How was it?"
Santosh thought about the bridge, the fallen cone, and that last smooth turn.
"Can we do it again?"
On the walk home, he carried Tiger under one arm.
A small blue ribbon was tied around the toy's paw.
It said: EXCELLENT CO-DRIVER.
Tiger, who had done absolutely none of the steering, seemed very pleased.

title: The Pencil That Draws Real Things
paragraphs: Scratchy, scratchy, scribble-scratch.
There was a small sound coming from under the sofa.
Rose got down on her knees and peeped underneath.
There, in the dust, lay a golden pencil.
She pulled it out and held it up to the light.
"Nick, look what I found!" she said.
"A shiny pencil."
Nick came over from the kitchen table, where Mummy was pouring tea.
He took the pencil and turned it round in his fingers.
"That's not one of ours," said Nick.
"Our pencils are all grey and chewed."
Rose wanted to know if it worked.
Nick wanted to know where it came from.
Shosh the fox sat on the table, watching with stitched-on eyes.
Rose found a scrap of paper.
She drew a butterfly, with orange wings and little round spots.
Then something amazing happened.
The butterfly lifted right off the page.
It flapped its wings and flew up into the kitchen.
"It's real!" shouted Rose.
"The pencil draws real things!"
The butterfly looped round the lamp.
It swooped past the window.
Then it landed straight on top of Mummy's head.
"Oh!" said Mummy, holding very still.
"There is a butterfly on my hair."
Mummy laughed, but when she turned round, her elbow bumped her teacup.
The cup tipped over, and tea spread across the table in a brown puddle.
"My tea," said Mummy.
"And my nice quiet kitchen."
The butterfly took off again.
It zoomed this way and that.
It landed on Shosh's nose, then bounced off and flew behind the curtains.
"We need to catch it," said Nick.
"But it's too fast for hands."
Rose thought for a moment.
Then she had an idea.
"Butterflies like flowers," she said.
"Draw a flower, Nick!
A big one!"
Nick took the pencil and drew a huge sunflower on the paper.
The flower rose up, real and golden, with a fat brown middle.
He held it high in the middle of the kitchen.
The butterfly peeked out from behind the curtain.
It saw the sunflower.
Slowly, slowly, it fluttered across the kitchen.
Then it folded its wings and settled on the flower's middle.
"Got it," whispered Nick, grinning.
"Now what?" asked Mummy, mopping the tea with a cloth.
"We can't keep a butterfly in the kitchen forever."
Rose looked at the window.
Then she looked at her paper.
She knew just what to do.
She took the pencil back from Nick.
On the paper she drew the garden, with green grass and a patch of flowers.
And in the middle of the garden she drew a little open window.
Mummy opened the real window wide.
Nick carried the sunflower over, butterfly and all, and held it outside.
The butterfly twitched its wings.
It saw the garden below, full of flowers just like the one it was sitting on.
It lifted off and floated away over the fence, into the sunshine.
"Bye bye, butterfly!" called Rose, waving.
Shosh the fox sat on the windowsill, and Rose sat Shosh's paw on the sill too, so Shosh could wave as well.
Mummy looked at the tea puddle, all gone now.
She looked at the golden pencil in Rose's hand.
"That's a clever pencil," said Mummy.
"But who is going to tidy up all these pencil marks?"
Rose smiled.
She drew a small yellow sponge on the paper.
The sponge popped up, real and soapy, and began wiping the table all by itself.
"Careful," said Nick, stepping back with a laugh.
"If she draws a hoover next, we'll all be out of a job!"
